passages.original: 3 Περὶ δὲ ἀναπνοῆς οἱ μὲν οὐ λέγουσι τίνος χάριν, ἀλλὰ μόνον ὃν τρόπον γίνεται, καθάπερ Ἐμπεδοκλῆς καὶ Δημόκριτος· οἱ δʼ οὐδὲ τὸν τρόπον ὅλως λέγουσιν, ἀλλʼ ὡς φανερῷ χρῶνται. δεῖ δὲ καὶ εἰ καταψύξεως χάριν, αὐτὸ τοῦτο διασαφῆσαι. εἰ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ἄνω τὸ θερμόν, οὐκ ἂν ἔτι δέοιτο κάτω. τὸ δὲ σύμφυτον πνεῦμα διʼ ὅλου, καὶ ἀρχὴ ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύμονος.
passages.english: Concerning respiration, some do not say for the sake of what it occurs, but only in what manner it comes about, as Empedocles and Democritus do; others do not state even the manner at all, but treat it as obvious. But if [it is] for the sake of cooling, one must make clear this very point. For if the heat is in the upper parts, it would no longer need [to go] downwards. But the connate breath [extends] throughout the whole [body], and [its] source is from the lung.
passages.notes: The leading "3" is a section number from the edition and is not translated. "Connate breath" renders σύμφυτον πνεῦμα, the innate pneuma. The text of this treatise is elliptical and probably corrupt in places. The sense of "would no longer need [to go] downwards" is uncertain: the argument seems to be that if the heat is in the upper body, breath would not need to travel to the lower parts.
